title: Strang's reason proves too much: by it God could foreknow no absolute contingent he had not decreed, which Strang denies
source_text: LX. Ratio autem ejus est, ut supra retulimus, quod nihil certo cognosci potest quod non sit certo verum: nihil autem certo verum est quod necessarium non sit vel absolute, vel ex hypothesi. Unde colligit futura conditionata non posse esse objectum scientiae divinae, quae infallibilis & certissima est, nisi in conditione includatur aliquid unde quod dicitur futurum necessario inferatur. Sed si haec ratio valeret, nullum contingens Deus praescire posset tanquam absolute futurum, nisi quod prius absolute futurum decrevisset: quod tamen non admittit Strangius, qui fatetur homines multa libere agere ad quae a Deo non praedeterminantur.
pass_a_gloss: LX. And his reason is, as we related above, that nothing can be certainly known which is not certainly true: but nothing is certainly true which is not necessary either absolutely, or by hypothesis. Whence he gathers that conditional futures cannot be the object of divine knowledge, which is infallible & most certain, unless in the condition something be included whence that which is said to be future is necessarily inferred. But if this reason were valid, God could foreknow no contingent as absolutely future, except what he had first decreed to be absolutely future: which yet Strang does not admit, who confesses that men freely do many things to which they are not predetermined by God.
pass_b_english: His reason, as reported above, is that nothing can be known with certainty that is not certainly true, and nothing is certainly true that is not necessary either absolutely or on a hypothesis. He concludes that conditional futures cannot be the object of God's knowledge, which is infallible and entirely certain, unless the condition includes something from which what is called future follows necessarily.

But if this argument held, God could foreknow no contingent thing as absolutely future except what he had first decreed to be absolutely future. Yet Strang does not accept that, since he grants that people freely do many things to which God does not predetermine them.

choices.why: Knowledge of what would happen under a condition; kept as the technical counterpart to middle knowledge.
